children: London's FTSE was muted on Friday but notched a second consecutive weekly gain, as declines in energy shares from weaker oil prices were offset by gains in banks and miners.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index
CURRENCYCOM:UK100
closed 0.14% higher at 10,695.25 points, leaving it in positive territory for the week. The midcap FTSE 250
climbed 0.44%, also marking a weekly gain.
Heavyweight banks (.FTNMX301010) climbed 1.3%, with Barclays
up 1.6%, while Lloyds Banking
and Standard Chartered
added around 1.7% and 2.5% respectively.
Precious metal miners
jumped 2% as gold and silver prices rose after dropping sharply earlier this week.
Oil prices eased after two sessions of gains as investors weighed hopes of a U.S.-Iran truce against risks to supply from escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Energy giant Shell
lost 0.8%.
was down 2.3%. Reuters reported on Thursday BP is weighing a potential acquisition of US-based Devon Energy's
operations in South Texas. HSBC upgraded the stock to "buy" from "hold".

Global government bond yields eased a touch after jumping earlier this week. The British benchmark 10-year gilt (GB10YT=RR) yield inched lower to 5.3810% after hitting a more than one-week high earlier this week.

A survey showed British consumer confidence unexpectedly struck a more than two-year high this month as households grew more optimistic about their personal finances, adding to recent signs of resilience in the economy.

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said that persistently high energy prices would make it harder for the central bank to leave interest rates on hold, underlining a recent shift in tone towards higher borrowing costs.
Investors are expecting at least one 25-basis-point hike by the BoE this year, according to data compiled by LSEG.
Among stocks, land and property regeneration company Harworth Group
rose 5.1% after Peel Holdings-backed Goodweather Holdings raised its final offer to 187 pence per share.
Oil and gas producer Capricorn Energy
gained 13.9% after Genel Energy
